newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta gears up for Euro-Med meeting.
newsitem.headline: Malta gears up for Euro-Med meeting.

text.p: Less than six months after taking power, Malta's new Labour government, which has frozen plans to take the island into the European Union, is preparing to host one of the biggest gatherings this year of European and Mediterranean foreign ministers.
Ministers from all EU and Mediterranean countries except Libya are expected to attend the Euro-Med conference in Valletta on April 15 and 16 in a follow-up to the 1995 Barcelona conference.
Foreign Minister George Vella has described the choice of Malta for the meeting as "vindication of the government's Euro-Mediterranean policies and policy of neutrality".
Malta's Labour administration, elected in October, wants a special relationship with the EU and an industrial free trade zone, instead of the membership sought by the former Nationalist government.

"Membership is not best way for Malta, given its particular circumstances, but we will seek the closest possible relations with the union in all areas that are mutually beneficial," Vella told the Maltese parliament last month.
At the same time his government is giving greater importance to Mediterranean affairs.
Vella said on Friday that during the April conference Malta planned to make practical proposals for cooperation between Europe and the Mediterranean.
Stressing the need for confidence-building measures, Vella said areas of cooperation could involve regional problems such as water, health and education.
"At this early stage it would be best to go for proposals which serve to bring countries closer together," he said.

He described the agenda of the Malta meeting as very wide, including political and security measures, economic and financial cooperation and cooperation in the social, cultural and educational sectors.

"The conference will help to create the right climate for problem-solving. It is encouraging to see that both Syria and Israel as well as Greece and Turkey will be attending the conference," he said, adding that Malta wanted to serve as a catalyst for cooperation between the region's north and south.
"Confidence building measures, preventive diplomacy and other non-military initiatives all fall in line with our foreign policy."
Vella said the EU Commission expected the conference would review progress made since it called the first Euro-Med conference in 1995.
